title: AI giant Anthropic's shares pop in debut after blockbuster IPO
description:
Shares in the AI juggernaut Anthropic are now trading on the stock market. They debuted Thursday, after a record-breaking IPO.

SCOTT DETROW, HOST: Shares in the AI juggernaut Anthropic are now trading on the stock market. They debuted today after a record-breaking IPO.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)ADENA FRIEDMAN: Today, Anthropic becomes a public company and begins trading on NASDAQ under the ticker symbol ANT.DETROW: The chair and CEO of NASDAQ celebrated the listing this morning. The CEO of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, had a big grin when he rang the opening bell.(SOUNDBITE OF BELL RINGING)DETROW: And speaking of Anthropic and speaking of money, here is where we do have to note that Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR. NPR's John Ruwitch is on the line from Silicon Valley with more from today. Hey, John.JOHN RUWITCH, BYLINE: Hey, Scott.DETROW: Run us through the numbers. How big was this?RUWITCH: It was big. Anthropic sold nearly a billion shares to the public and sold others at the same time to a handful of big tech firms in what's known as a private placement. The total haul for the company, its founders, was more than $107 billion, with a B. The IPO alone was the biggest in history, blowing past SpaceX's listing from June, which had set the previous record.You know, IPOs are kind of a two-step process. The company sells the shares at a fixed price to investors who apply in advance to get in on the IPO. That price was 83 bucks, which was higher than expected. And then the shares start trading on the stock market, which is what happened today, and they started out with a bang, opening up 34% from the IPO price. Now, they've come down off of the high over the course of the trading day, but they did end trading still well above the IPO price.DETROW: What's interesting here is there's so many worries about AI right now, and one of the big worries is that, you know, the industry is possibly in a big bubble. Given that, why do you think investors were so eager to snap up these shares?RUWITCH: Well, AI is changing the way people do a lot of things, from searching for the internet to developing new medicines, and Anthropic's right at the center of it - right? - with its Claude AI models. They are among the most advanced models in the world, and they're popular. Today, Anthropic became the first publicly traded big AI lab that only does AI. SpaceX is one of its AI rivals, but it does other things like put satellites into orbit. So prior to today, if the average person wanted investment exposure to AI, it was less direct. They had buy shares in companies that make chips, for instance, or software or satellites.You're right. There is tension around AI. People are worried about data centers. They're worried about losing their jobs to AI, worried about AI going rogue or spiraling out of control. And investors have been concerned about all that money pouring into AI, whether or not it's justified.DETROW: What did the company's leadership have to say about those risks this morning when trading got underway?RUWITCH: Yeah. CEO Dario Amodei tackled this head-on in his remarks while ringing that opening bell at the NASDAQ. You know, he's long been outspoken about AI's risks. In fact, he and a handful of others left competitor, OpenAI, and founded this company five years ago because they were worried about AI's safety. Today, he said going public won't change that mission.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)DARIO AMODEI: We will not bend to either business nor political pressure. Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing.RUWITCH: He pledged to be careful about the pace of training and releasing new models and to take as long as necessary to make sure that they're safe and that they remain under control. And he said he hopes Anthropic can lead, quote, "a race to the top" by making the right choices on safety and being a successful company.DETROW: That sounds like something that's very easy to say and very hard to do. I mean...RUWITCH: Yeah.DETROW: ...What all does that entail?RUWITCH: A lot. I mean, the future for AI companies like Anthropic depends partly on the rise of really useful applications for AI, including some nobody's imagined yet. Anthropic has committed to spending hundreds of billions of dollars on data centers to build and run powerful new AI models to try to get there, and it'll take revenue for that.DETROW: Where will that money come from, though?RUWITCH: You know, at the moment, most of Anthropic's revenue appears to be coming from companies. But as with every new technology, success or failure hinges on how quickly people adopt it. You know, one analyst I talked to used radios and washing machines as an example. They were new technologies once, and people adopted them at very different rates. Radio spread quickly into American homes. Washing machines took decades. So the question is, will AI be more like the radio or the washing machine?DETROW: Well, we're very glad that the radio technology spread. That is NPR's John Ruwitch reporting from Silicon Valley. Thank you so much.RUWITCH: You're welcome. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. Visit our website terms of use and permissions pages at www.npr.org for further information.
